title: Prednisone and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Steroids?
excerpt: Can you drink on prednisone? How steroids and alcohol overlap on your stomach, blood sugar, sleep, and bones, short burst vs long-term use, and when to call a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on prednisone? How steroids and alcohol affect your stomach, blood sugar, and sleep, short burst vs long-term use, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** prednisone and alcohol don't cause a sudden, dangerous reaction the way some antibiotics do. For most healthy adults on a short course, an occasional single drink is unlikely to cause harm, and many doctors are fine with that. The problem is that prednisone and alcohol share several of the same side effects. Both irritate the stomach lining, both push blood sugar around, both disturb sleep and mood, both weaken the immune system, and over months both thin your bones. Stack them and each of those problems gets worse. The more you drink, and the longer you take prednisone, the more those overlaps matter.

**The quick rules:** If you're on a short "burst" (usually around five days to two weeks), keep alcohol to an occasional single drink or skip it until you finish. If you take prednisone for weeks, months, or long term, ask your doctor what's safe for you, because the bone, stomach, and blood-sugar risks build up over time. Never skip or delay a dose so you can drink, and never stop prednisone suddenly on your own after more than a few weeks. If you have diabetes, a history of stomach ulcers, or you also take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin, be especially careful and talk to your doctor before drinking at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance about prednisone (a corticosteroid, often just called a steroid). It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed it and knows why you're taking it. **Talk to your doctor before drinking if** you take prednisone for more than a couple of weeks, you have diabetes or high blood sugar, you've had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, you take blood thinners or anti-inflammatory painkillers, you have liver disease, or you've been told you have thinning bones. **Get medical help right away if** you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, have severe stomach pain, feel extremely thirsty and are urinating far more than usual, have signs of infection with a fever, or notice sudden severe changes in mood or thinking. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Prednisone and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Prednisone is a man-made version of cortisol, the stress hormone your adrenal glands make every day. Your liver converts prednisone into its active form, prednisolone, which then dials down inflammation and calms an overactive immune system. That's why it's prescribed for so many different things: asthma flares, allergic reactions, poison ivy, gout attacks, back pain from an inflamed nerve, flares of rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and many more.

The important thing to understand is that **there's no single chemical clash between prednisone and alcohol.** Alcohol doesn't stop prednisone from working in any well-documented way, and prednisone doesn't make alcohol toxic. Instead, the two drugs push on the same body systems in the same direction. Think of it as two people leaning on the same wobbly table. Either one alone is usually fine. Both together is when things tip.

Here are the systems where they overlap:

1. **Your stomach and gut lining.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid. Corticosteroids can make the lining more vulnerable and slow healing. Together, they raise the chance of gastritis (an inflamed stomach), ulcers, and bleeding.
2. **Your blood sugar.** Prednisone raises blood sugar, sometimes a lot. Alcohol can first spike it (sugary drinks and mixers) and then drop it (alcohol blocks the liver from releasing stored sugar). The result is a less predictable ride.
3. **Your sleep and mood.** Prednisone commonly causes insomnia, restlessness, irritability, and mood swings. Alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night and can worsen anxiety and low mood the next day.
4. **Your immune system.** Prednisone deliberately suppresses parts of your immune response. Heavy drinking also weakens immune defenses. Combined, you may be more prone to infections.
5. **Your bones.** Long-term steroid use is a well-known cause of bone thinning (osteoporosis). Regular heavy drinking is too. This one is mostly about long-term use, not a one-week course.
6. **Your blood pressure and fluid balance.** Prednisone can make you hold onto salt and water and raise blood pressure. Regular heavy drinking also raises blood pressure.

None of this means one glass of wine with dinner will hurt you. It means the dose of alcohol and the length of your prednisone course are what decide how much risk you're adding.

## What Official Guidance Actually Says

The prescribing information for prednisone doesn't list alcohol as a strict contraindication (meaning it doesn't say "never combine these"). Major health references, including pharmacist-written drug guides, generally advise limiting alcohol while taking corticosteroids because of the stomach, blood-sugar, and bone risks, rather than forbidding it outright.

In practice, that leaves the decision to you and your prescriber, and the right answer depends on your situation. A healthy 30-year-old on a five-day burst for poison ivy is in a very different position from someone with type 2 diabetes on long-term prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis. That's why "is it safe?" doesn't have one answer, and why the most useful thing you can do is understand which risks apply to you.

## Short Burst vs Long-Term Prednisone: Why It Changes the Answer

This is the single biggest factor, so it's worth splitting the two clearly.

### Short courses (a "burst" or quick taper)

A burst is a short, usually higher-dose course, often around five days to two weeks, sometimes with a quick taper at the end. It's used for things like asthma flares, bronchitis with wheezing, bad allergic reactions, poison ivy, gout attacks, or a pinched nerve.

On a short course, the long-term risks (bone loss, adrenal suppression, cataracts) mostly don't come into play. The side effects you're more likely to notice are the fast ones: trouble sleeping, feeling wired or irritable, increased appetite, stomach upset, and higher blood sugar. Those are exactly the ones alcohol makes worse.

For most healthy adults on a burst, a single drink on an occasional evening is unlikely to cause a real problem. Several drinks, or drinking every night of the course, is a different story. You're more likely to get stomach pain or reflux, sleep even worse than prednisone already makes you, and feel rougher the next day. And whatever you're being treated for may heal more slowly. If the burst is for asthma, alcohol (and the sulfites in some wines) can be a trigger for some people. If it's for gout, alcohol, especially beer, is a known gout trigger and works directly against the treatment.

Many people decide the simplest choice is to skip alcohol for the few days of the course. That's a reasonable call and costs you very little.

### Long-term or repeated courses

If you take prednisone for more than a few weeks, at any dose, or you get several courses a year, the picture changes. This is where the slow-building overlaps matter most:

- **Bones.** Long-term steroids are one of the most common causes of medication-related osteoporosis. Regular heavy drinking also reduces bone density and raises fall risk. Your doctor may already be checking your bones or prescribing calcium, vitamin D, or a bone-protecting medicine. Heavy drinking undercuts all of that. Our guide to [alcohol and bone health](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-bone-health-complete-skeletal-impact-analysis) covers the alcohol side in more detail.
- **Stomach.** The longer you're exposed to both, the more chances for gastritis or an ulcer to develop.
- **Blood sugar.** Long-term steroids can push some people into prediabetes or diabetes ("steroid-induced diabetes"). Regular drinking adds calories and makes glucose control harder.
- **Infections.** Long-term immune suppression plus heavy drinking is a riskier mix, especially for chest infections.
- **Liver.** Prednisone is processed by the liver, and so is alcohol. In people with existing liver disease, both the medicine and the alcohol need a doctor's oversight.

If you're on long-term prednisone, don't guess. Ask your prescriber directly: "How much alcohol, if any, is reasonable for me?" They know your dose, your other medicines, and your test results.

## The Stomach Risk: Ulcers and Bleeding

This is the risk that comes up most often, and it's real, so here's the plain version.

Corticosteroids on their own carry a modest increase in the risk of stomach and intestinal problems. The risk climbs noticeably when they're combined with other things that damage the stomach lining. The two biggest are **NSAIDs** (ibuprofen, naproxen, high-dose aspirin) and **alcohol**.

That matters because a lot of people on prednisone also have pain. It's common to reach for ibuprofen for a headache or a hangover without thinking. Prednisone plus an NSAID plus alcohol is the combination most worth avoiding, because each one hits the stomach lining in a different way. If you need a painkiller while on prednisone, ask your pharmacist which one is safest for you. Our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains why NSAIDs and drinking are a rough pairing even without a steroid in the mix.

Ways to lower the stomach risk if you do have a drink:

- **Take prednisone with food,** usually with breakfast. This is standard advice anyway.
- **Never drink on an empty stomach.** Eat a real meal first.
- **Keep it to one drink** and sip it slowly.
- **Skip NSAIDs** unless your doctor has said they're okay.
- **Avoid very strong drinks** like straight spirits and shots, which are harsher on the stomach lining.

### Warning signs of a stomach bleed

These are uncommon but serious. Get medical help right away if you notice:

- Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, sticky, tar-like stools, or bright red blood in the stool
- Sudden, severe, or persistent pain in the upper belly
- Feeling faint, dizzy, or unusually pale and weak

A little mild indigestion after a drink is common and usually passes. Persistent burning pain that keeps coming back while you're on prednisone is worth mentioning to your doctor even if it isn't severe. For more on what's normal and what isn't, see our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking).

## The Blood Sugar Problem

Prednisone makes the liver release more glucose and makes your body's cells respond less to insulin. In people without diabetes, that usually means a mild, temporary rise that goes away after the course. In people with diabetes or prediabetes, blood sugar can climb high enough to need extra medication or insulin while they're on the steroid.

Alcohol complicates this in two opposite directions:

- **Up:** beer, sweet cocktails, cider, sweet wine, and sugary mixers add a load of fast sugar on top of the prednisone effect.
- **Down:** while your liver is busy processing alcohol, it's worse at releasing stored sugar. In people who take insulin or certain diabetes pills (like sulfonylureas), this can cause low blood sugar hours later, sometimes overnight.

So you can get a high, then a low, at a time when the steroid has already made your numbers harder to read. The symptoms of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) can also be mistaken for simply being drunk.

**If you have diabetes and are on prednisone,** talk to your doctor before drinking at all, check your blood sugar more often, never drink without eating, and make sure someone you're with knows you have diabetes. Our [alcohol and diabetes guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) goes into the alcohol side in more depth.

**If you don't have diabetes,** watch for signs your blood sugar may be running high on prednisone: unusual thirst, peeing much more than usual, blurred vision, or extreme tiredness. If you notice these, tell your doctor. Sugary drinks will make them worse.

## Sleep, Mood, and "Roid Rage"

Insomnia is one of the most common complaints on prednisone, especially at higher doses. Many people also feel restless, wired, irritable, or emotional. Less often, steroids cause more serious mood changes such as anxiety, depression, or, rarely, confusion or psychosis, usually at higher doses.

Alcohol can seem like a fix for steroid insomnia, because it makes you drowsy. It isn't. Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up sleep later in the night, cuts into REM sleep, and often wakes you early. On top of steroid insomnia, that can leave you with very little real rest. Alcohol can also lower your guard and make irritability or mood swings harder to manage, and next-day anxiety ("hangxiety") tends to be worse when you're already running on poor sleep.

Better options for steroid insomnia:

- **Take your dose in the morning,** usually with breakfast, unless your doctor has told you otherwise. This roughly matches your body's own cortisol rhythm and is the single most helpful habit for sleep on prednisone.
- **Cut caffeine after lunch.** Prednisone already has you wired.
- **Ask about splitting or timing** if insomnia is severe. Don't change your dose schedule without checking first.

**Get help right away** if you or someone close to you notices severe mood changes on prednisone: feeling hopeless, thoughts of self-harm, extreme agitation, confusion, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there. These are known, treatable steroid effects, and your doctor needs to know. Alcohol will make them worse, not better. In the US you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline any time.

## Infections and Healing

Prednisone works partly by calming your immune system. That's the point when you're treating an allergic or autoimmune problem, but it also means you may fight infections less well and heal more slowly, especially on higher doses or long courses.

Heavy drinking also weakens immune defenses, both right after a binge and over time. Our guide to [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) covers how. Combining the two isn't a reason to panic over one drink, but it's a good reason not to drink heavily while you're on a steroid, and especially not if the reason you're on prednisone involves an infection, like a chest infection with wheezing.

Tell your doctor promptly if you develop a fever, chills, a cough that's getting worse, painful urination, or a wound that looks red, hot, or swollen while you're taking prednisone. Steroids can also hide some signs of infection, so don't wait for it to feel severe.

## Can You Drink the Night Before or After Your Last Dose?

Prednisone itself clears your body fairly quickly. Its active form is mostly gone within about a day. But its effects on blood sugar, sleep, and mood can linger a little after the last tablet, and if you were on it for weeks, your body may need time to recover its own cortisol production.

For a short burst, waiting until a day or two after your last dose before drinking more than a little is a sensible, cautious approach. For a long course or a taper, ask your doctor, because the end of a taper is when some people feel tired, achy, or low as their adrenal glands catch up. Alcohol won't help with that.

## Don't Skip a Dose to Drink

People sometimes think it's safer to skip a prednisone dose on a night out. It isn't, for two reasons.

First, missing doses can let the inflammation you're treating flare back up, which defeats the purpose of the course.

Second, and more important, **if you've been on prednisone for more than about three weeks, your body may have reduced its own cortisol production.** Stopping suddenly, or missing several doses, can cause adrenal insufficiency: severe tiredness, weakness, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, low blood pressure, and in serious cases, collapse. This is why longer courses are tapered down gradually instead of stopped. If you vomit after drinking and can't keep your prednisone down, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice, especially on a long course.

The safe rule is simple: take every dose on schedule, and if alcohol and the dose seem to conflict, adjust the alcohol, not the medicine.

## Prednisone Hangovers: Why They Can Feel Worse

There's no good evidence that prednisone changes how drunk you get or how quickly your blood alcohol rises. But many people say hangovers feel worse while they're on it, and the reasons are easy to see:

- **You're already sleeping badly,** and alcohol makes that worse. Poor sleep is a major driver of how bad a hangover feels.
- **Your stomach is more sensitive,** so nausea, reflux, and stomach pain hit harder.
- **Your blood sugar is less stable,** which can add to shakiness, fatigue, and brain fog.
- **Your mood is more fragile,** so next-day anxiety or irritability can be stronger.

If you do wake up with a hangover while on prednisone, be careful with what you take for it. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin add to the stomach risk. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but has its own alcohol warnings for the liver; our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the safe limits. Water, a gentle meal, and rest are the safest first steps. If in doubt, ask a pharmacist, and tell them you're on prednisone.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You should talk to your doctor before drinking at all on prednisone if any of these apply:

- **You have diabetes or prediabetes,** or your blood sugar has run high on steroids before.
- **You've had a stomach ulcer, gastritis, or GI bleeding,** or you have reflux that's hard to control.
- **You take NSAIDs, aspirin, or blood thinners** like warfarin or apixaban.
- **You're on long-term prednisone,** or you get several courses a year.
- **You have osteoporosis or thinning bones,** or you're at high risk of falls.
- **You have liver disease** or have been told your liver tests are abnormal.
- **You have high blood pressure or heart failure,** since both prednisone and alcohol can raise blood pressure and fluid retention.
- **You have a history of depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder,** since both substances can affect mood.
- **You're older,** since bone, stomach, and fall risks rise with age.
- **You find it hard to keep drinking to one or two,** or you usually drink most days. In that case, your doctor really needs to know how much you drink to treat you safely. Being honest about it is part of getting the right care, not a judgment.

## If You Do Drink: A Practical Checklist

For a healthy adult on a short course whose doctor hasn't told them to avoid alcohol entirely:

1. **Keep it to one drink,** and not every night.
2. **Eat a real meal first,** and take your prednisone with breakfast as usual.
3. **Choose lower-sugar drinks.** A glass of dry wine or a light beer is easier on blood sugar than a sweet cocktail. Sugary mixers stack on top of the steroid's glucose effect.
4. **Alternate with water.** Dehydration makes everything worse.
5. **Skip ibuprofen and naproxen** for the headache the next day unless your doctor said they're fine.
6. **Stop early in the evening** to protect your already fragile sleep.
7. **Watch for warning signs:** black stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, extreme thirst, or major mood changes. Get help if you see them.
8. **Take your next dose on time,** no matter what.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

If you're reading this because you have an event coming up during a prednisone course, it's natural to wonder about hangover supplements. Here's an honest view.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven, and **there is no good evidence that DHM reduces any of the specific risks of combining prednisone with alcohol.** It won't protect your stomach lining, steady your blood sugar, or fix steroid insomnia, and it isn't a reason to drink more than you otherwise would.

DHM also hasn't been studied alongside prednisone. Supplements can interact with medicines, so **check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM** or any other supplement while you're on a steroid. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what's known and what isn't.

If you get the go-ahead and want to try it on a night when you do drink, commonly chosen options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take. But for someone on prednisone, the habits in our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover), especially drinking less, eating first, and hydrating, matter far more than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Prednisone and alcohol don't have a dramatic, immediate reaction, which is why the "is it safe?" question gets so many different answers online. The real issue is overlap: both drugs strain your stomach, blood sugar, sleep, mood, immune system, and, over time, your bones. On a short course, an occasional single drink with food is unlikely to harm most healthy adults, though many people simply skip alcohol for those few days. On a long course, or if you have diabetes, ulcers, thinning bones, or take NSAIDs, the risks add up, and your doctor should guide the decision. Whatever you choose, take every dose on schedule and never stop a long course suddenly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?**

There's no strict ban, and for most healthy adults on a short course, an occasional single drink with food is unlikely to cause harm. But prednisone and alcohol share side effects, including stomach irritation, higher blood sugar, poor sleep, and mood changes, so drinking more than a little makes those worse. If you take prednisone long term, have diabetes or a history of ulcers, or take NSAIDs, ask your doctor first.

**How long after taking prednisone can I drink alcohol?**

Prednisone clears your body fairly quickly, but its effects on blood sugar, sleep, and mood can linger briefly. After a short burst, waiting a day or two after the last dose before drinking more than a little is a cautious approach. After a long course or taper, ask your doctor, because your body may still be recovering its own cortisol production.

**Does alcohol make prednisone less effective?**

There's no good evidence that a moderate amount of alcohol stops prednisone from working. But alcohol can work against what prednisone is treating. It's a common trigger for gout attacks and can trigger asthma in some people, and heavy drinking slows healing and weakens the immune system. Skipping doses to drink is the bigger threat to the treatment.

**Can prednisone and alcohol cause stomach ulcers?**

They can raise the risk, especially together. Both can irritate or weaken the stomach lining, and the risk rises further if you also take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin. Take prednisone with food, don't drink on an empty stomach, and avoid NSAIDs unless your doctor approves them. Get help right away for black stools, vomiting blood, or severe stomach pain.

**Is it safe to drink on a 5-day prednisone burst?**

For most healthy adults, one drink on an occasional evening during a short burst is unlikely to cause a real problem. Heavy drinking or drinking every night is more likely to worsen insomnia, stomach upset, and blood sugar, and may slow your recovery from whatever the burst is treating. Many people simply skip alcohol for the few days of the course.

**Does prednisone make hangovers worse?**

Many people report that it does. There's no good evidence that prednisone changes how drunk you get, but it can worsen the things that make hangovers feel bad: poor sleep, a sensitive stomach, unstable blood sugar, and a more fragile mood. If you need a painkiller the next day, ask a pharmacist, since ibuprofen and naproxen add to the stomach risk.

**Should I skip my prednisone dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Take every dose on schedule. Missing doses can let your condition flare, and if you've been on prednisone for more than about three weeks, suddenly stopping or missing several doses can cause adrenal insufficiency, which can be serious. If alcohol and your dose conflict, adjust the alcohol, not the medicine.

**Can I drink on prednisone if I have diabetes?**

Talk to your doctor first. Prednisone raises blood sugar, and alcohol can push it higher with sugary drinks and then lower hours later, especially if you take insulin or certain diabetes pills. If you do drink, eat first, choose lower-sugar drinks, check your blood sugar more often, and make sure someone with you knows you have diabetes.
